Apple Squeezed These Chip Suppliers for Years. AI Is Helping Them Get Even.
 
Plus, Weil Gotshal says it is shutting its doors, and we take you inside the $311 million land grab to create one of America’s priciest homes
 
 
EMIL LENDOF/WSJ, ISTOCK
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

For years, Apple bullied flash-memory makers into hefty discounts, paying pennies for iPhone storage that it resold to customers for dollars. One aggrieved sales executive even shot his old iPod with a rifle. Now, the tables have turned.

 

The AI boom has sent tech giants on an unprecedented buying spree, quintupling flash prices and shattering Apple’s supply-chain leverage.

 

According to TechInsights, Apple is on track to spend $25 billion on flash storage this year—up from $6 billion in 2025 for roughly the same volume. Tim Cook likened escalating memory-chip prices to a “100-year flood.”

 

This morning, we examine how the AI arms race caught Cupertino off guard and is threatening the company’s steep profit margins.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Vice President JD Vance is engaging one of Iran’s most powerful hard-liners to revive peace negotiations even as President Trump threatens to restart the war, U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter said.

 

• Leaders at Weil, Gotshal & Manges said they plan to dissolve the law firm, capping a stunning fall for one of the most venerable names in the industry.

 

• The U.S. expelled Cuba’s foreign minister after heated ​words and a battle over a cellphone at the United Nations.

 

• In Texas, Hispanic voters upset about the economy and immigration policies are set to decide key Senate and House races.

• Alphabet still has the ingredients to win in an AI pullback, writes Asa Fitch.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

Tech giants are ramping up resistance to ICE in a bid to avoid Democratic scrutiny.

 

The Trump administration has increased its use of subpoenas to seek information from big technology companies about users critical of its immigration policies. Now, with Democrats pushing to regain power in the midterm elections, Silicon Valley is stepping up its quiet resistance. Board members and top executives inside companies like Google and Meta are trying to insulate their firms from potential future Democratic-led congressional investigations and respond to user and employee concerns, while still placating the Trump administration, report Emily Glazer, Georgia Wells and Hannah Critchfield.

 

5.

 

Flávio Bolsonaro fled Brazil with the help of decoys, a private jet and a friend in the White House.

 

Less than 24 hours after losing the presidential election, he appeared to vanish into a convoy of four dark cars. After pulling away from his home in Brasília on Monday evening, the vehicles split in different directions, leaving journalists and authorities scrambling to determine which one carried Bolsonaro. By the next afternoon, his allies were telling reporters he had already reached Florida. His arrival followed an extraordinary effort by influential Trump allies, senior U.S. officials and Argentina’s president to help Bolsonaro fly to the U.S. and secure entry, despite a Brazilian court order barring him from leaving the country. Trump personally approved admitting Bolsonaro and his family to the U.S., report Vera Bergengruen, Samantha Pearson, Ryan Dubé and Philip Wegmann.

The Trump administration is building a stock portfolio that spans more than 40 companies.
